<h1 id="Paper-012-%E2%80%94-MODES-Toolbox:-Metrics-of-Open-Ended-Evolution">Paper 012 — MODES Toolbox: Metrics of Open-Ended Evolution<a class="anchor-link" href="#Paper-012-%E2%80%94-MODES-Toolbox:-Metrics-of-Open-Ended-Evolution">¶</a></h1><p><strong>Dolson, E., Vostinar, A. E., Wiser, M. J., Ofria, C. (2019).</strong> "The MODES Toolbox: Measurements of Open-Ended Dynamics in Evolving Systems." <em>Artificial Life</em> <strong>25</strong>(1):50–73. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1162/artl_a_00280">doi:10.1162/artl_a_00280</a></p>
<h2 id="Summary">Summary<a class="anchor-link" href="#Summary">¶</a></h2><p>The MODES toolbox provides four metrics for detecting open-ended evolution: <strong>Change</strong>, <strong>Novelty</strong>, <strong>Complexity</strong>, and <strong>Ecology</strong>. This notebook validates them on three test systems: an open-ended random walk, a closed fixed-point attractor, and NK landscape evolution.</p>
<ul>
<li>Adapted from <code>control/modes/modes_toolbox.py</code></li>
<li>Provenance: <code>src/provenance/experiments.rs</code> — <code>MODES_PROVENANCE</code></li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="cell border-box-sizing text_cell rendered"><div class="inner_cell">
<div class="text_cell_render border-box-sizing rendered_html">
<h2 id="Background">Background<a class="anchor-link" href="#Background">¶</a></h2><p><strong>MODES</strong> (Measurements of Open-Ended Dynamics in Evolving Systems) treats open-endedness along four complementary axes:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Change</strong> — rate at which new types appear in the system (cumulative diversity dynamics).</li>
<li><strong>Novelty</strong> — how different emerging types are from types already present (not just minor variants).</li>
<li><strong>Complexity</strong> — whether phenotypic or genotypic complexity trends upward over time (e.g., via a linear fit).</li>
<li><strong>Ecology</strong> — Shannon diversity and evenness of the type abundance distribution at each time step.</li>
</ol>
<p>Together, these metrics help distinguish systems that keep producing new, diverse structure from those that collapse to a small, stable set of states.</p>
<h3 id="BarraCUDA-/-ecoPrimals-connection">BarraCUDA / ecoPrimals connection<a class="anchor-link" href="#BarraCUDA-/-ecoPrimals-connection">¶</a></h3><p>The same quantities can be computed on <strong>BarraCUDA</strong> evolution traces: shader variants and architecture search produce time series of “types” and abundances. Distances for novelty map to elementwise differences and reductions; ecological indices use logarithms and sums over populations—operations aligned with GPU reduction patterns. This notebook’s synthetic systems stand in for those traces while matching the paper’s validation logic.</p>
</div>
</div>

<h3 id="Key-findings">Key findings<a class="anchor-link" href="#Key-findings">¶</a></h3><ul>
<li><strong>MODES discriminates system types</strong>: the open random-walk system consistently scores above the closed fixed-point system on change, novelty, ecology, and complexity trend.</li>
<li><strong>Four complementary axes</strong>: no single scalar captures open-endedness; change, novelty, complexity slope, and ecological evenness respond differently to the same run.</li>
<li><strong>NK as intermediate</strong>: the NK landscape typically sits between open and closed on key scalars, matching the paper’s use of structured but bounded search spaces.</li>
<li><strong>BarraCUDA / ecoPrimals</strong>: the same pipeline can score real evolution logs (shaders, genomes, populations) using reductions and distances familiar from GPU kernels.</li>
</ul>
